description:
Pyra

Pyra is a geospatial exploration platform designed to harmonize MODIS and VIIRS satellite active-fire hotspot observations into a unified, time-aware experience. Our goal is to make satellite fire data easier to explore, compare, and understand across locations and historical periods through an interactive 3D globe so users can explore hotspot detections, travel back in time and compare observations from different periods and satellite sources.
summary: Pyra is a web app that turns NASA's MODIS and VIIRS satellite hotspot records into an explorable burning-activity calendar on an interactive 3D globe. Users lock an area by drawing it, entering coordinates, searching a place name, or using their current location — then drag a timeline or calendar through 25 years of harmonized detections (2000–present) and watch the globe, counts, charts, and comparisons update together. A burning-activity calendar with accessible color ramps shows which months and years burned most, and the selected period is compared against the historical median with clearly defined anomalies. Every observation carries source attribution, freshness, and limitations, and any selection exports to CSV. Built for the Space Apps "MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots" challenge, Pyra matters because consistent, explainable fire-activity records help responders, scientists, and land managers see patterns and change over time with detections presented honestly and never as confirmed fires or forecasts.
details:
What is it about?
Pyra is a web app that answers one question at a time: what did NASA's MODIS and VIIRS satellites observe, in this area, during this period? The user locks an area on an interactive 3D globe by drawing it, entering coordinates, searching a place name, or a one-tap current-location fix, then drags a timeline or a burning-activity calendar through 25 years of harmonized hotspot detections (2000–present). One query drives the whole screen: globe markers, counts, activity chart, calendar, historical comparison, and details panel all render the same response snapshot. Scrubbing runs a real historical query and atomically replaces the markers and stale responses can never overwrite newer ones. Every observation carries its sensor of origin, observation vs. ingestion time, confidence with source-defined meaning, FRP with units, and known limitations and any selection exports to a CSV that matches the on-screen filters exactly.

Benefits

- One consistent record instead of two sensor silos: MODIS continuity plus VIIRS detail, combined under a documented harmonization method (docs/harmonization.md), with comparability warnings where sensors differ.

- Reproducible: every number on screen traces to a documented query, freshness timestamp, and downloadable CSV.

Intended impact

Give early-warning responders, scientists, land managers, and firefighters a shared, explainable view of fire-activity patterns and change over time — which months and years burned most, and how current activity compares with the historical median — while refusing to overclaim: detections are never framed as confirmed fires, burned area, perimeters, or forecasts.

Tools, languages, hardware, software

- Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, custom Three.js globe (lazy-loaded, capped marker layer), Recharts for the activity chart; Vitest/Testing Library and Playwright for tests. Deployed as a static site on Vercel.

- Backend: Python, FastAPI, Pydantic, psycopg with per-tier connection pooling, PostgreSQL with PostGIS (Supabase) holding the bounded FIRMS ingest, plus a bounded in-process cache and a rolling ingest/gap-fill worker. Deployed on Render as a single process.

- Data: NASA FIRMS (MODIS C6.1, VIIRS 375 m NRT) via server-side ingest.

Creativity

The calendar is the query control: scrubbing months fires the same request path as the timeline, so history feels tactile rather than tabular. The harmonized record is presented with its seams showing sensor of origin, method doc and comparability warnings.

Factors considered

Phone-first budgets (lazy globe or chart, marker caps, no heavy UI kits), accessibility (keyboard-operable calendar, list/table alternative to the globe, announced state changes, color-never-alone encoding), privacy (location only on explicit tap, never tracked or stored), single-origin simplicity (split only where deployment required it, with an explicit CORS allowlist), and the hard rule that the app must never read as an emergency service or advise approaching fires.
